terminal.description: A shell in your workspace. `node src/catalogue.ts` runs the catalogue, and `npm run types` checks its types.

tasks.title: Name the properties of a tin
tasks.description:
Under `// Task 1` in `src/catalogue.ts`, `cell` gives one property of a tin as text. Rafe typed `field` as `string`, and the compiler refuses the body. Write a type alias called `TinField`, with `export` in front, for the names of the properties of `Tin`, made from `Tin` itself. Then use it as the type of `field`. Leave the body as it is.

Check refuses `any` and `as` in your lines, and reads them for the word `type` in front of `TinField` and for `TinField` on `field`. It compiles code of its own: every property name of a tin must be a `TinField`, while a name a tin does not have, or any text at all, must be refused. Then it adds a property to `Tin` in its own copy, and expects `TinField` to take in its name. It calls `cell` with tins of its own.
nextSteps: Run `npm run types` and read the error on the body of `cell` to the end.
Read the lesson's part on the names of the properties.
Write `TinField` above `cell`, made from `Tin`, and use it as the type of `field`.
hints: The error says a `string` cannot be used to read from a `Tin`: any text could be passed, and most text names no property. `field` should only allow the names a tin has.
Writing the names out by hand as a union works today, and stops working the day `Tin` gets a property. There is a word that gives the names of the properties of a type, and follows it.
`export type TinField = keyof Tin`, then `field: TinField` in the first line of `cell`.

tasks.title: Read the type of one property
tasks.description:
Under `// Task 2`, `tinsOfSize` gives the tins of one size. Rafe typed `size` as `number`, so a call with a size the shop does not sell compiles and finds nothing. Write a type alias called `Size`, with `export` in front, for the type of the `size` property of `Tin`, read from `Tin` itself. Then use it as the type of `size`. Leave the body as it is.

Check refuses `any` and `as` in your lines, and reads them for the word `type` in front of `Size` and for `Size` on `size`. It compiles code of its own: every size a tin can have must be a `Size`, while a size the shop does not sell, or text, must be refused. Then it gives `Tin` a new size in its own copy, and expects `Size` to take it in. It calls `tinsOfSize` with tins of its own.
nextSteps: Look at the `size` property of `Tin`: what values does its type allow?
Read the lesson's part on reading the type of one property.
Write `Size` above `tinsOfSize`, read from `Tin`, and use it as the type of `size`.
hints: `number` allows 300, and every other number. The type of `size` in `Tin` allows only three, and that is the type this parameter should have.
Square brackets after a type, with the name of a property in quotes, give the type of that property. It changes when the property's type changes.
`export type Size = Tin['size']`, then `size: Size` in the first line of `tinsOfSize`.

tasks.title: Write a function that changes a tin
tasks.description:
Under `// Task 3`, write a function called `updateTin`, with `export` in front, from the word `function` to its closing brace. It takes a tin and the changes to make to it: any of the properties of a tin, each with its own type, and none of them required. It gives back a new tin with the changes made, and leaves the tin it was given as it was. Make the type of the changes from `Tin`, so it follows `Tin`, and write every type. Then take away the `//` in front of the lines at the end, to see it run.

Check refuses `any` and `as` in your lines, and reads `updateTin` for its result type. It compiles code of its own: changes to one property, to a few and to none must compile, while a change of the wrong type, to a property a tin does not have, or to a size the shop does not sell must be refused. Then it adds a property and a size to `Tin` in its own copy, and expects the changes to take them in. It calls `updateTin` with tins of its own, and checks the tin it passed is left as it was.
nextSteps: Write the first line: the name, a tin, the changes and the result type.
Read the lesson's part on a type with every property optional, and use it for the changes.
Give back a new object with the properties of the tin and then the changes.
Take away the `//` in front of the last lines, and run both commands.
hints: `Tin` as the type of the changes asks for every property, so `{ stock: 9 }` is refused. A copy of `Tin` with a question mark on every property works until `Tin` changes.
There is a type that takes a type and makes every one of its properties optional, keeping their types. In an object, `...` copies properties, and a later one wins.
`export function updateTin(tin: Tin, changes: Partial<Tin>): Tin {` with `return { ...tin, ...changes }` inside.

tasks.title: Make some of a tin, or all but one
tasks.description:
Under `// Task 4`, Rafe copied `Tin` by hand twice more. A `NewTin` is what the stock form sends: everything a tin has but its `id`, which `withId` gives it. A `ShelfLabel` has only the `blend` and the `size`, all a label needs. Write both again, made from `Tin`, so they follow it. Keep their names, with `export` in front, and leave the functions as they are.

Check refuses `any` and `as` in your lines, and reads them for the word `type` in front of both names. It compiles code of its own: a new tin without an id, a label and a whole tin passed as a label must compile, while a new tin with an id or without its stock, and a label without a blend, with a price or with a size the shop does not sell must be refused. Then it adds a property and a size to `Tin` in its own copy: a `NewTin` must take in both, and a `ShelfLabel` only the size. It calls both functions with values of its own.
nextSteps: Read the lesson's part on keeping some properties, or all but some.
Ask, for each type: is it a few properties of a tin, or all of them but a few?
Write each again from `Tin`, naming only the properties that decide it.
hints: Both copies are right today. Check adds a property to `Tin`: a new tin from the form has it too, while a label still has only two. A copy written by hand does neither.
One type keeps only the properties you name, and another keeps all of them but the ones you name. The names go in quotes, joined by `|` when there are more than one.
`export type NewTin = Omit<Tin, 'id'>` and `export type ShelfLabel = Pick<Tin, 'blend' | 'size'>`.
